items.prompt: What does "redundancy" mean in this unit's sense?
choices: Running more than one independent copy of a system so the failure of one doesn't take down the whole thing
Removing duplicate code from a codebase
Adding extra logging so failures are easier to diagnose
Running automated tests before every deploy
items.explanation: Redundancy is specifically about independent copies of a running system — not code cleanliness, logging, or testing practice.
items.reference:
🌎 Single region — one copy, one point of failure
🌍🌎 Redundant — more than one independent copy

Why: a single copy, however well-built, has the region it runs in as an unavoidable single point of failure.

items.prompt: The Scenario's checkout service passed every code review and test suite, yet still had a single point of failure. What was it?
choices: The region it ran in — there was no second running copy anywhere else
A missing unit test for the checkout flow
An unpatched security vulnerability
A slow database query
items.explanation: The service's own code quality was never the issue — the single point of failure was structural: only one region had a running copy of the system.
items.reference:
🌎 Single region — one copy, one point of failure
🌍🌎 Redundant — more than one independent copy

Why: a single copy, however well-built, has the region it runs in as an unavoidable single point of failure.

items.prompt: Why can't application-level code quality alone prevent the kind of outage in this unit's Scenario?
choices: Because the failure was in the region's infrastructure, not in any code the application team wrote
Because the application had too many dependencies
Because the team didn't write enough tests
Because the checkout service used the wrong programming language
items.explanation: The application had no bugs — the outage came from the underlying region failing, which no amount of application code quality addresses.
items.reference:
🌎 Single region — one copy, one point of failure
🌍🌎 Redundant — more than one independent copy

Why: a single copy, however well-built, has the region it runs in as an unavoidable single point of failure.

items.prompt: What is "failover"?
choices: Shifting traffic away from a failed copy of a system and onto a healthy one
Restarting a crashed process automatically
Rolling back a bad deployment to the previous version
Compressing data before sending it over the network
items.explanation: Failover is specifically about redirecting traffic to a healthy copy — not process restart, deployment rollback, or compression.
items.reference:
🔻 Region fails — traffic still aimed at it
↪️ Failover — traffic redirected to a healthy region

Why: redundancy only helps if something actually redirects traffic once a copy fails.

items.prompt: Having a second, healthy copy of a system running in another region, with nothing redirecting traffic to it during an outage, gives you what?
choices: Redundancy without failover — the healthy copy exists but isn't being used
A fully working disaster recovery setup
An active-active deployment
Zero RPO automatically
items.explanation: Redundancy (a second copy existing) and failover (traffic actually reaching it) are two different things — one without the other still leaves users hitting the failed region.
items.reference:
🔻 Region fails — traffic still aimed at it
↪️ Failover — traffic redirected to a healthy region

Why: redundancy only helps if something actually redirects traffic once a copy fails.

items.prompt: What is "disaster recovery" (DR) as used in this unit?
choices: The broader plan for restoring service after a large-scale failure, such as a full region loss
A tool for recovering deleted files
The process of writing incident postmortems
A backup of a single server's configuration files
items.explanation: DR is the overall plan for restoring service after a large-scale failure — broader than any single mechanism like a health check or a DNS update.
items.reference: Why: DR is the umbrella plan a region-loss failover sits inside, not one specific mechanism.

items.prompt: What does RTO (Recovery Time Objective) measure?
choices: How long the system is allowed to be down before service is restored
How much data the system is allowed to lose
How many regions a system runs in
How fast a single API request responds
items.explanation: RTO is a duration of allowed downtime, not a data-loss measure, a region count, or a latency figure.
items.reference:
⏱️ RTO — how long down is allowed to be
💾 RPO — how much data is allowed to be lost

Why: the Scenario's 6-hour outage was an RTO failure — the system took far longer than any reasonable objective to come back.

items.prompt: A system comes back online 6 hours after the Scenario's region outage began. Against a 5-minute RTO, was this a successful disaster recovery?
choices: No — the actual downtime badly exceeded the RTO, regardless of the system eventually recovering
Yes — the system did eventually recover, and that's all RTO measures
Yes, as long as no data was lost
It depends only on whether the region itself came back online
items.explanation: RTO is judged against the actual time taken, not just whether recovery eventually happened — 6 hours against a 5-minute objective is a clear miss.
items.reference:
⏱️ RTO — how long down is allowed to be
💾 RPO — how much data is allowed to be lost

Why: the Scenario's 6-hour outage was an RTO failure — the system took far longer than any reasonable objective to come back.

items.prompt: Which of these is an RTO, expressed correctly?
choices: "Service must be restored within 5 minutes of a region failure"
"At most 30 seconds of writes may be lost"
"The system runs in 3 regions"
"Health checks run every 10 seconds"
"Replicas use synchronous replication"
items.explanation: RTO is a downtime duration objective. "30 seconds of writes" describes RPO, and the others describe implementation details, not objectives.
items.reference:
⏱️ RTO — how long down is allowed to be
💾 RPO — how much data is allowed to be lost

Why: the Scenario's 6-hour outage was an RTO failure — the system took far longer than any reasonable objective to come back.

items.prompt: What does RPO (Recovery Point Objective) measure?
choices: How much data the system is allowed to lose, measured as a span of time
How long the system is allowed to be down
How many independent regions the system runs in
The maximum acceptable response latency
items.explanation: RPO is about how much data can be lost, expressed as a time span ("at most the last N seconds of writes") — not about downtime, region count, or latency.
items.reference:
⏱️ RTO — how long down is allowed to be
💾 RPO — how much data is allowed to be lost

Why: RPO answers "how much of the last few moments of data can we afford to lose," separate from downtime.

items.prompt: An RPO of 30 seconds means, after a failover, what is guaranteed?
choices: At most the last 30 seconds of writes before the failure may be gone
The system will be back online within 30 seconds
The failover will complete in 30 seconds or less
Health checks will detect the failure within 30 seconds
items.explanation: RPO is a data-loss bound, not a time-to-recover bound — a 30-second RPO says nothing about how fast the system comes back, only how much recent data might be missing when it does.
items.reference:
⏱️ RTO — how long down is allowed to be
💾 RPO — how much data is allowed to be lost

Why: RPO answers "how much of the last few moments of data can we afford to lose," separate from downtime.

items.prompt: In an active-passive setup, what is the standby region doing during normal operation?
choices: Standing by, ready to take over, but not serving live traffic
Serving an equal share of live traffic alongside the primary
Running a completely different application
Nothing is running there until a failure occurs
items.explanation: Active-passive means the standby is running and kept ready, just not serving live traffic — it isn't idle-and-unprovisioned, and it isn't sharing live load either.
items.reference:
🅰️ Active-passive — one region serves traffic, one stands by
🅰️🅱️ Active-active — more than one region serves traffic at once

Why: the trade is idle standby capacity (lower cost) vs. always-on multi-region serving (near-zero failover gap).

items.prompt: Which setup typically has a lower RTO: active-passive or active-active, and why?
choices: Active-active — the other regions are already serving traffic, so there's little or no failover gap when one fails
Active-passive — a dedicated standby is always faster to promote than a region already under live load
They're identical, since RTO only depends on the failover router
Active-passive, because it has lower normal-day cost
items.explanation: In active-active, the surviving regions are already serving traffic, so there's no promotion step to wait on — active-passive requires a failover to actually happen first, which takes time.
items.reference:
🅰️ Active-passive — one region serves traffic, one stands by
🅰️🅱️ Active-active — more than one region serves traffic at once

Why: the trade is idle standby capacity (lower cost) vs. always-on multi-region serving (near-zero failover gap).

items.prompt: Why do many systems default to asynchronous replication despite it allowing some data loss on failover?
choices: Because the primary can acknowledge writes immediately without waiting for a replica, keeping write latency low
Because asynchronous replication guarantees zero data loss
Because it's required for active-active deployments
Because it eliminates the need for health checks
items.explanation: Asynchronous replication trades some RPO risk for lower write latency, since the primary doesn't wait on the replica before acknowledging a write.
items.reference:
Asyncfast writes, RPO = lag at failure
Syncnear-zero RPO, slower writes

Why: RPO is set by how far the replica trailed the primary at the exact moment of failure.

items.prompt: A system uses synchronous replication. What does it give up compared to asynchronous replication?
choices: Lower write latency — and writes can stall if the replica is unreachable
Any protection against data loss on failover
The ability to run in more than one region
The ability to use health checks at all
items.explanation: Synchronous replication trades write latency (and availability, if the replica is unreachable) for a near-zero RPO — it doesn't affect health checks or multi-region capability directly.
items.reference:
Asyncfast writes, RPO = lag at failure
Syncnear-zero RPO, slower writes

Why: RPO is set by how far the replica trailed the primary at the exact moment of failure.

items.prompt: What does semi-synchronous replication offer as a middle ground?
choices: The primary waits for at least one of several replicas to confirm, balancing latency and RPO
It replicates half the data synchronously and half asynchronously
It only replicates during off-peak hours
It removes the need for a quorum
items.explanation: Semi-synchronous replication requires confirmation from at least one replica (not all), landing between full synchronous and full asynchronous on both latency and RPO.
items.reference:
Asyncfast writes, RPO = lag at failure
Syncnear-zero RPO, slower writes

Why: RPO is set by how far the replica trailed the primary at the exact moment of failure.

items.prompt: What is "split-brain"?
choices: A state where more than one region believes it's the writable primary at the same time, producing diverging data
A crash caused by a null pointer in the failover router
The state right after a region is correctly promoted to primary
A health checker reporting inconsistent results over time
items.explanation: Split-brain specifically means two (or more) regions both acting as primary simultaneously, which causes writes to diverge — it's not a crash or a single flaky report.
items.reference:
🧠🧠 Split-brain — two regions both think they're primary
🗳️ Quorum — majority agreement prevents it

Why: reconciling two diverged copies after the fact can be worse than the original outage.

items.prompt: What specific situation is most likely to trigger split-brain?
choices: A network partition makes the primary unreachable from the health checker, even though the primary is still running fine
The primary region runs out of disk space
A deploy introduces a new bug in the application code
Write traffic to the primary suddenly drops to zero
items.explanation: A network partition can make a perfectly healthy primary look unreachable to a checker, which can trigger a wrongful promotion of the standby while the original primary is still accepting writes.
items.reference:
🧠🧠 Split-brain — two regions both think they're primary
🗳️ Quorum — majority agreement prevents it

Why: reconciling two diverged copies after the fact can be worse than the original outage.

items.prompt: Put the three steps of a failover in the correct order.
choices: Detect the region is down, decide to promote a standby, redirect traffic to it
Redirect traffic, then detect the region is down, then decide whether to promote
Decide to promote a standby, redirect traffic, then detect whether the original region is still down
There is no fixed order — all three happen simultaneously
items.explanation: The order matters: you can't decide to promote before detecting a failure, and you can't redirect traffic before deciding where it should go.
items.reference:
Detect → Decide → Redirect.

Why: RTO is the sum of all three steps — a fast router can't compensate for a slow detector.

items.prompt: A team lowers their DNS TTL from 300 seconds to 10 seconds and says their RTO problem is solved. What's missing from that claim?
choices: It only speeds up the redirect step — the detect and decide steps could still be slow
DNS TTL has no effect on RTO at all
Lowering DNS TTL actually increases RTO
DNS TTL only affects RPO, not RTO
items.explanation: RTO is detect + decide + redirect. A shorter DNS TTL only improves the redirect step; it does nothing for how long detection or promotion takes.
items.reference:
Detect → Decide → Redirect.

Why: RTO is the sum of all three steps — a fast router can't compensate for a slow detector.

items.prompt: Why is a quorum typically made of an odd number of voters?
choices: So a majority is always possible, avoiding a tie that leaves no clear verdict
Odd numbers are cheaper to provision than even numbers
It's required by DNS providers
It guarantees synchronous replication
items.explanation: An odd total makes an even split impossible, so a majority verdict can always be reached instead of deadlocking on a tie.
items.reference:
🧠🧠 Split-brain — two regions both think they're primary
🗳️ Quorum — majority agreement prevents it

Why: a majority requirement means a partition can produce at most one side with a majority.

items.prompt: With a 5-voter quorum, how many voters must agree before a failover decision is made?
choices: 3 — a majority
5 — unanimous agreement
1 — any single voter is enough
2 — a plurality is sufficient
items.explanation: Quorum requires a majority: floor(5/2) + 1 = 3 out of 5, not unanimity and not a single voter.
items.reference:
🧠🧠 Split-brain — two regions both think they're primary
🗳️ Quorum — majority agreement prevents it

Why: a majority requirement means a partition can produce at most one side with a majority.

items.prompt: A 4-voter setup reports 2 voters reachable and 2 unreachable. What verdict should a correctly implemented quorum check return?
choices: No verdict at all — neither side reaches the majority of 3
"unhealthy", since half the voters report unreachable
"healthy", since half the voters report reachable
It should pick whichever side reported first
items.explanation: With 4 voters, quorum is floor(4/2) + 1 = 3. A 2-2 split reaches neither threshold, so the correct behavior is to decline to act rather than guess.
items.reference:
🧠🧠 Split-brain — two regions both think they're primary
🗳️ Quorum — majority agreement prevents it

Why: a majority requirement means a partition can produce at most one side with a majority.

items.prompt: Two regions are each individually redundant, but both depend on the same central identity service. What does this do to their failure independence?
choices: It breaks it — a failure in the shared identity service can take both regions down together
Nothing — regions are always independent of each other by definition
It improves independence, since the identity service adds another layer
It only matters for RPO, not for availability
items.explanation: Shared dependencies (identity, DNS, a certificate authority) are correlated failure points — a failure there defeats the independence that multi-region redundancy relies on.
items.reference:
🌍 Region A
🌎 Region B
🔗 Shared dependency — breaks independence for both

Why: availability math assumes independent failures; a shared dependency makes that assumption false.

items.prompt: Why does "blast radius" matter when designing redundancy, beyond just counting how many regions exist?
choices: A shared dependency across regions can expand the blast radius of a single failure to cover all of them at once
Blast radius only applies to physical data centers, not cloud regions
More regions always shrinks blast radius, with no exceptions
Blast radius is only relevant to RTO, never to RPO
items.explanation: Counting regions alone assumes independence; a shared dependency can widen a single failure's blast radius to include every region that depends on it.
items.reference:
🌍 Region A
🌎 Region B
🔗 Shared dependency — breaks independence for both

Why: availability math assumes independent failures; a shared dependency makes that assumption false.

items.prompt: A system claims 3-region redundancy, but all 3 regions issue TLS certificates from the same certificate authority integration, which has an outage. What happens?
choices: All 3 regions can be affected simultaneously, despite being otherwise independent
Only the region that requested the certificate most recently is affected
Nothing — certificate authorities are unrelated to regional redundancy
The quorum automatically routes around the shared dependency
items.explanation: A shared dependency like a certificate authority integration is a correlated failure point — if it fails, every region relying on it can be affected at once, regardless of how independent the regions otherwise are.
items.reference:
🌍 Region A
🌎 Region B
🔗 Shared dependency — breaks independence for both

Why: availability math assumes independent failures; a shared dependency makes that assumption false.

items.prompt: Implement quorumVerdict(voterReports) which returns "healthy" if a majority of voters report the region reachable, "unhealthy" if a majority report it unreachable, and "no-quorum" if neither side has a majority.

tests.description: 3/3 reachable is healthy
2/3 unreachable is unhealthy
even split with no majority is no-quorum
5-voter majority of 3 unreachable is unhealthy

items.explanation: Computing quorum as a true majority (floor(total/2) + 1) and returning "no-quorum" when neither side reaches it is what prevents a single voter's disagreement, or an even split, from producing a wrongful failover decision.
items.reference:
🗳️🗳️🗳️ 3 voters — quorum is 2
❓ Even split — no majority, refuse to act

Why: guessing on an ambiguous verdict is the split-brain risk in disguise — refusing to act is the safe default.

items.prompt: Fix FailoverRouter so it only fails over to the standby after 3 consecutive "unhealthy" verdicts, and resets the counter on a "healthy" verdict.

tests.description: does not fail over before threshold
tests.expr: expect((() => { const r = new FailoverRouter(["a", "b"]); r.reportVerdict("unhealthy"); r.reportVerdict("unhealthy"); return r.primary; })()).toBe("a")

tests.description: fails over at threshold
tests.expr: expect((() => { const r = new FailoverRouter(["a", "b"]); r.reportVerdict("unhealthy"); r.reportVerdict("unhealthy"); r.reportVerdict("unhealthy"); return r.primary; })()).toBe("b")

tests.description: healthy verdict resets the counter
tests.expr: expect((() => { const r = new FailoverRouter(["a", "b"]); r.reportVerdict("unhealthy"); r.reportVerdict("unhealthy"); r.reportVerdict("healthy"); r.reportVerdict("unhealthy"); r.reportVerdict("unhealthy"); return r.primary; })()).toBe("a")

items.explanation: Requiring several consecutive unhealthy verdicts before failing over, and resetting on any healthy verdict, is what keeps a single transient blip from triggering an unnecessary failover — at the direct cost of adding detection cycles to the RTO.
items.reference:
1️⃣2️⃣3️⃣ 3 consecutive unhealthy — triggers failover
✅ 1 healthy — resets the counter

Why: a threshold trades detection speed for avoiding false alarms — the same trade-off named in L2's detect step.

tests.description: fails over once threshold of 2 is reached
tests.expr: expect((() => { const r = new FailoverRouter(["a", "b"]); r.reportVerdict("unhealthy"); r.reportVerdict("unhealthy"); return r.primary; })()).toBe("b")

Why: a threshold trades detection speed for avoiding false alarms — the same trade-off named in L2's detect step.

items.prompt: Implement estimateRpoExposure(lagSamplesMs, writesPerSecond) returning { rpoSeconds, worstCaseLostWrites }, using the worst (maximum) sampled lag, not the average.

tests.description: uses the worst sample, not the average
computes worst-case lost writes from the worst lag
handles a single sample

items.explanation: Using the worst sampled lag (not the average) matters because failover can happen at any moment, including during a lag spike — an estimate built on the average would understate the real worst-case exposure.
items.reference:
📊 Average lag — looks safe, hides spikes
📈 Worst lag — the real RPO exposure

Why: a failure can land during the unlucky moment lag briefly spiked, not during typical conditions.

items.prompt: Implement combinedAnnualDowntimeMinutes(perRegionFailureProbability, numRegions), assuming independent regions where the system is down only if every region fails simultaneously.

tests.description: 1 region matches the raw probability scaled to minutes/year
2 independent regions multiply probabilities
more regions means lower combined downtime

items.explanation: Independent regions' failure probabilities multiply, not add, so going from one region to two can cut downtime by orders of magnitude — but this assumes true independence, which breaks if regions share a dependency.
items.reference:
✖️ Independent failures — probabilities multiply
🔗 Shared dependency — breaks the assumption

Why: both regions have to fail during an overlapping window, which is far less likely than either failing alone.

items.prompt: Implement pickPrimaryRegion(regions), where regions is an array of { name, healthy } in priority order. Return the name of the first healthy region, or null if none are healthy.

tests.description: returns the first healthy region in priority order
tests.expr: expect(pickPrimaryRegion([{ name: "a", healthy: false }, { name: "b", healthy: true }, { name: "c", healthy: true }])).toBe("b")

tests.description: returns the highest-priority region if it's healthy
tests.expr: expect(pickPrimaryRegion([{ name: "a", healthy: true }, { name: "b", healthy: true }])).toBe("a")

tests.description: returns null when no region is healthy
tests.expr: expect(pickPrimaryRegion([{ name: "a", healthy: false }, { name: "b", healthy: false }])).toBe(null)

items.explanation: Scanning in priority order and returning the first healthy region (or null if none) is the actual selection logic a redirect step needs — it's a plain search, not a probability calculation.
items.reference:
1️⃣ Region A (priority 1)
2️⃣ Region B (priority 2)

Why: redirect needs to know exactly which region traffic should land on once a verdict is in.
